blocks.text: This closing topic of the module covers evaluating an agent as a whole, an entire multi-step trajectory rather than a single prompt and response, bringing together planning, reflection, tool selection, routing, memory, and multi-step reasoning, all covered earlier in this module, into a genuine evaluation framework.

This topic covers task success rate as the primary metric, evaluating trajectory efficiency, tool selection and execution accuracy, planning quality, and building a realistic test suite covering common agent failure modes.
1. Why Agent Evaluation Differs From Single-Prompt Evaluation

blocks.alt: Why Agent Evaluation Differs From Single-Prompt Evaluation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807746-25380312.png

Evaluating a single prompt, covered in the general Prompt Iteration topic from an earlier module, means comparing one input against one output, evaluating an agent means assessing an entire multi-step trajectory, many actions, many decisions, against whether the original goal was genuinely accomplished.

blocks.alt: Why Agent Evaluation Differs From Single-Prompt Evaluation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807747-320064492.png
2. Task Success Rate as the Primary Metric

blocks.alt: Task Success Rate as the Primary Metric
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807747-226316980.png

The most fundamental agent evaluation metric is simply, across a set of realistic test tasks, how often does the agent actually accomplish the stated goal, this connects directly to the metric-driven iteration process covered in an earlier module, applied here at the level of a complete trajectory rather than a single response.
3. Evaluating Trajectory Efficiency
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807748-89786350.png

Beyond simply succeeding or failing, an agent trajectory can be evaluated on efficiency, did it accomplish the goal in a reasonable number of steps, or did it take redundant actions, repeat a failed approach unnecessarily, or wander through unnecessary tool calls before reaching the actual answer.

blocks.text: 4. Evaluating Tool Selection and Execution Accuracy

blocks.alt: Evaluating Tool Selection and Execution Accuracy
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807748-465513151.png

This connects directly to tool selection prompts and tool execution prompts, both covered earlier in this module, tracking how often the agent chose the genuinely correct tool for each step, and how often it formatted and executed that tool call correctly, breaks down overall agent performance into more specific, actionable components.
5. Evaluating Planning and Re-Planning Quality
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807748-709652284.png

This connects directly to planning prompts and reflection prompts, both covered earlier in this module, evaluating whether an agent initial plan was actually reasonable given the goal, and separately, whether re-planning triggered by reflection genuinely improved the trajectory when it happened, gives insight into these two specific pieces of the overall system.

blocks.title: Breaking down evaluation by component reveals where to actually improve
blocks.content: A low overall task success rate could stem from poor planning, poor tool selection, or poor execution, evaluating each component separately, rather than only the final outcome, reveals specifically which part of the system most needs improvement.

blocks.text: 6. Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems Specifically

This connects to multi-agent communication, covered earlier in this module, for a system involving several communicating agents, evaluation also needs to check whether communication between them actually worked correctly, not just whether the final combined output was good, isolating a communication failure from a reasoning failure in either individual agent.
7. Building a Realistic Agent Test Suite

blocks.alt: Building a Realistic Agent Test Suite
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473807968-117772444.png

A genuinely useful agent test suite includes not just straightforward, easy tasks, but also tasks likely to trigger the specific failure modes covered across this module, an unavailable tool, a step that genuinely fails and needs recovery, a task requiring the agent to route or hand off between specialized roles.
8. Common Agent Failure Modes Worth Testing For

Across this module, several recurring failure patterns are worth deliberately testing against, an agent that does not adapt its plan when a step fails, one that loops on the same unproductive action, one that loses coherence over a long trajectory, and one that mishandles communication with another agent, each connects to a specific topic covered earlier in this module.
9. This Module Is Now Complete

This closes out the Agent Prompting module, planning, reflection, tool selection, routing, memory, multi-step reasoning, multi-agent communication, dynamic prompt generation, tool execution, and now agent evaluation, together forming a complete toolkit for building and validating agents that take real, multi-step actions, the next module, Prompt Security, covers defending against deliberate adversarial attempts to manipulate a prompt, a concern that becomes especially important once an agent can take genuine real-world actions.
Worked Example

A team building a task automation agent measures only overall task success rate, seeing sixty percent, without further breakdown, they cannot tell whether the failures come from bad planning, wrong tool selection, or execution errors.

Breaking evaluation down by component reveals planning is actually reasonable in nearly every case, but tool selection accuracy is only seventy percent, largely due to two tools with overlapping, poorly differentiated descriptions, exactly the kind of issue covered in the earlier Tool Selection Prompts topic, fixing those specific descriptions raises overall task success meaningfully more than any other single change the team considered.
Common Mistakes

items: Measuring only overall task success rate without breaking down evaluation by component to find the actual root cause
Testing an agent only against straightforward, easy tasks that never trigger the failure modes covered in this module
Not evaluating trajectory efficiency, missing cases where the agent succeeds but through a wasteful, redundant path
Evaluating a multi-agent system only by its final output, missing communication specific failures between the individual agents

blocks.text: Practice

Design an evaluation plan for an agent task you have designed or could design, including an overall task success metric, a component level breakdown covering planning, tool selection, and execution, and at least two test cases deliberately designed to trigger a specific failure mode covered in this module.
Key Takeaway

Agent evaluation assesses an entire multi-step trajectory against task success, trajectory efficiency, and component level accuracy in planning, tool selection, and execution, requiring a test suite that deliberately covers common agent failure modes rather than only straightforward tasks, and breaking evaluation down by component is what actually reveals where a struggling agent most needs improvement.
